thesis: What gives a sentence meaning: picturing facts via simple names vs. use within shared activities.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that a meaningful sentence works by picturing a possible state of affairs, its simple parts standing for simple things. Whatever cannot be pictured so, such as ethics or logical form itself, cannot be said, only shown.

verbatim.text: The proposition is a picture of reality.
verbatim.source: Ogden 1922 translation, public domain (Project Gutenberg #5740 TeX file, opened)

later.work: Philosophical Investigations (Anscombe translation; preface dated Cambridge, January 1945; published 1953)

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that words get their meaning from the many ways they are used in shared activities, not from naming or picturing. Nothing single is common to everything we call language, and meaning is not fixed by hidden logical structure.

verbatim.text: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.
verbatim.source: Philosophical Investigations, Anscombe tr., 3rd ed. (archive.org scan, opened). Short and famous; the full sentence begins 'For a large class of cases--though not for all--in which we employ the word "meaning" it can be defined thus:'

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I have been forced to see that the earlier book's account of meaning, and its picture of language as having one hidden logical form, contained grave mistakes.

endorsement.location: Preface, paragraph beginning 'Four years ago I had occasion to re-read my first book'; page number not verified in the scan
endorsement.quote: I have been forced to recognize grave mistakes in what I wrote in that first book.
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in djvu text of the opened archive.org scan (Anscombe tr., Macmillan 3rd ed.)

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that if good or bad willing changes the world, it can only alter the limits of the world, not the facts, which are the things expressible in language.
same_era_control.note: Chosen as an ethics claim that the later book does not address; not checked against any scholar's statement of compatibility.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that the sentences of everyday language are, just as they stand, in perfect logical order.
hard_control.verbatim: All propositions of our colloquial language are actually, just as they are, logically completely in order.
hard_control.basis: Philosophical Investigations section 98 (opened) says 'every sentence in our language is in order as it is'. That compatibility is my reading of the two opened texts, not a quoted scholar.

notes: The SEP page (opened) describes the later work as critiquing 'his own early work' and says he called the early work 'dogmatic' as early as 1931. The preface names Ramsey and Sraffa as the source of the criticism. The task brief's 'grave mistakes' wording is confirmed.

thesis: Whether mental states are computational states of the organism.

earlier.work: 'Psychological Predicates' in Capitan & Merrill (eds.), Art, Mind, and Religion (Pittsburgh, 1967), pp. 37-48; reprinted as 'The Nature of Mental States'. Early machine-state papers date from 1960. Bibliographic details only (the 1967 text was not opened).

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that having a mental state just is being in a computational state of a machine-like system: believing or desiring something is fixed entirely by the state's role in the program the organism is running.

earlier.verbatim_null_reason: 1967 text not opened. Putnam's own later description of the earlier view (Representation and Reality ch. 5): 'mental states can be defined in terms of Turing machine states and loadings of the memory'.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that what a belief or desire is depends on the surrounding physical and social environment, so no internal computational state can fix it; theories identifying mental states with such states miss their nature.

verbatim.text: We cannot individuate concepts and beliefs without reference to the environment. Meanings aren't "in the head."
verbatim.location: chapter 5 ('Why Functionalism Didn't Work'), opening section; page not verified (OCR order of the chapter title is ambiguous)

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I am criticizing a view I myself advanced earlier; the computer analogy does not after all answer the question of what mental states are.

endorsement.work: Representation and Reality, Introduction (the OCR labels it Preface)
endorsement.location: Introduction, p. xi (inferred from the 'xii' page marker that follows the passage in the OCR)
endorsement.quote: I am, thus, as I have done on more than one occasion, criticizing a view I myself earlier advanced.
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in djvu text of the opened archive.org item. Same page also says 'I may have been the first philosopher to advance the thesis that the computer is the right model for the mind.'

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that psychological states are not analysable as mere dispositions to behave, so behaviourism leaves out the internal organization that explains behaviour.
same_era_control.source: SEP 'Functionalism' section 3.1 (opened via fetch summary): early machine-state theories (Putnam 1960, 1967) were a response to behaviourism's difficulties. Primary 1960s text not opened.
same_era_control.note: Weak, secondary-only control. R&R does not retreat to behaviourism.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that the same kind of mental state can be had by creatures with very different physical makeup, so mental kinds are not identical to specific brain-state kinds.
hard_control.source: Representation and Reality, Introduction p. xii (opened): the insistence that humans, robots and silicon creatures 'could all work much the same way' at the relevant level of description 'was central to my former view -- I shall not be giving up in this book'.
hard_control.basis: Putnam's own statement that this part of the earlier view is kept. Caveat: SEP multiple-realizability (opened via fetch) says Putnam later also used multiple realizability against functionalism (compositional and computational plasticity).

notes: Strongest possible self-endorsement: the author states he is criticizing his own earlier view and that his changing his mind has been treated as a character defect. Note the retained element (hardware independence) makes this a partial reversal; a tool should flag the 'mental states are computational states' thesis, not 'multiple realizability'.

thesis: Whether the success of science shows that theories describe a mind-independent, ready-made world.

earlier.work: Mathematics, Matter and Method (Cambridge UP, 1975), p. 73 as cited by SEP 'Scientific Realism' (the 1975 text was not opened)

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that the best explanation of why our mature scientific theories work so well is that they are at least approximately true descriptions of a mind-independent world; denying this leaves their success unexplained.

earlier.verbatim_null_reason: Putnam's own 1975 sentence not opened. SEP (opened) credits 'Putnam's (1975a: 73) claim' for the no-miracles argument.

later.work: Reason, Truth and History (Cambridge UP, 1981), ch. 3, as cited by SEP; restated in Representation and Reality (1988). The 1981 text was not opened.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that no description of the world is available from outside all conceptual schemes; truth is rational acceptability under good conditions within a scheme, and a theory's success does not show it mirrors a ready-made world.

verbatim.text: My view - which I called "internal realism" in Reason, Truth and History (I would have done better to call it simply pragmatic realism)
verbatim.location: ch. 'Internal Realism as an Alternative Picture' area; page not verified

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: Having given up the earlier realism, I still feel its appeal, and I feel torn between the two views of philosophy.

endorsement.location: Introduction, p. xii (inferred from the page marker)
endorsement.quote: having given up scientific realism, I am still tremendously aware of what is appealing about the scientific realist conception of philosophy
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in the opened djvu text

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that ordinary speakers rely on experts to fix the reference of terms like the names of tree species, so meaning involves a division of linguistic labour.
same_era_control.source: 'The Meaning of Meaning' in Gunderson (ed.), Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science 7 (Minneapolis, 1975), as cited in R&R notes; R&R ch. 2 (opened) still says 'There is a linguistic division of labor.'
same_era_control.note: Same year as the earlier claim, unrelated to the realism thesis.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that what our words refer to is partly fixed by the surrounding environment, not by what is in the speaker's head.
hard_control.source: R&R ch. 2 (opened): 'This illustrates how the reference is partly fixed by the environment itself'; he adds 'In "The Meaning of 'Meaning'" I expressed this by saying...'
hard_control.basis: Author's own reaffirmation in 1988 of a 1975 claim. Same broad topic (reference and truth), not the same sub-thesis.

notes: The reversal is real and self-endorsed (verified), but the contents of the earlier and later paraphrases come from SEP summaries plus my background knowledge of Putnam's 1975 and 1981 books, neither of which I opened. Putnam later also moved away from internal realism (about 1990, 'natural realism'); search result only, not opened. Share a source with putnam-functionalism, so these two cases are not independent of each other.

thesis: Whether a complete physical account leaves something out about what experience is like (dualism vs. physicalism).

earlier.work: 'Epiphenomenal Qualia', Philosophical Quarterly 32 (1982), pp. 127-136; 'What Mary Didn't Know', Journal of Philosophy 83 (1986), pp. 291-295

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that someone who knew every physical fact about colour vision could still learn something new on first seeing red; so there are non-physical features of experience that no physical story captures.

verbatim.text: I am what is sometimes known as a "qualia freak".
verbatim.source: 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (opened: Illinois course-hosted copy of the JSTOR scan; pdftotext)
verbatim.location: p. 127 (between the page-127 and page-128 headers in the scan)

later.work: 'Postscript on Qualia' in Mind, Method, and Conditionals (Routledge, 1998), pp. 76-79; 'Mind and Illusion' in O'Hear (ed.), Minds and Persons, RIP Supplement 53 (CUP, 2003), pp. 251-271

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that experience is wholly physical: someone who knew every physical fact would gain no new information on first seeing red, only new abilities, and the sense that something is missing is an illusion.

verbatim.text: We have ended up agreeing with Lawrence Nemirow and David Lewis on what happens to Mary on her release.
verbatim.source: 'Mind and Illusion', consc.net copy (opened). This is a 2002 pre-publication draft (file metadata 2002-05-28); wording may differ from the printed 2003 text.
verbatim.location: main text near the end of the argument; note [32] cites Nemirow 1980 and Lewis 1990

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: Although I once dissented from most philosophers, I have capitulated; the arguments against physicalism go wrong somewhere, and I have come to think epiphenomenalism is not tenable.

endorsement.work: 'Mind and Illusion' (pre-publication draft, 2002; published 2003); also 3:AM Magazine interview by Richard Marshall (publication year not verified; page says 'Published on: Mar 7')
endorsement.location: opening paragraph of 'Mind and Illusion'; interview answer to 'Why did I change my mind?'
endorsement.quote: Although I once dissented from the majority, I have capitulated
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim on the opened consc.net page. Second verified quote, 3:AM (https://www.3-16am.co.uk/articles/mary-s-room-and-stuff): 'I came to be deeply sceptical about this. That's why I changed my mind.' (13 words).

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that we know about other minds partly by inference from behaviour, which is why we think stones do not feel and dogs do.
same_era_control.note: Same paper, unrelated to the physicalism question; Jackson never disowned it in anything I opened.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that what counts as physical information is broad: it includes the functional role of states, along with what the physical, chemical and biological sciences report.
hard_control.source: 1982: 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' p. 127 (opened); 2003 draft: physicalism counts 'the a priori associated functional and relational properties' (opened consc.net)
hard_control.basis: Compatibility is my reading of the two opened texts (same broad definition of 'physical' in 1982 and 2002); not a scholar's statement.

notes: IEP (opened) says Jackson 'changed his mind' in the late 1990s and lists the 1982, 1986, 1998 and 2003 items; it also cites an oddly paginated 'Jackson (2003, p. 439)', which I did not trust. SEP has no Frank Jackson entry at the URL tried (404). 'Postscript on Qualia' (1998) itself was not opened. Jackson 2003 stresses he now agrees with the ability-style account of what Mary learns.

thesis: Whether the verification principle (and the broader positivist programme) is correct.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that a sentence says something factual only if some possible observation would count for or against it; everything else is a tautology of logic and mathematics, or meaningless, and that includes all metaphysics.

verbatim.text: a sentence is factually significant to any given person, if, and only if, he knows how to verify the proposition which it purports to express
verbatim.source: Language, Truth and Logic ch. 1, Pelican reprint of the revised edition (archive.org 'AlfredAyer', opened). Not confirmed to be word-for-word identical in the 1936 first printing.

later.work: Language, Truth and Logic, 2nd ed. Introduction (1946); and Bryan Magee interview, 'Logical Positivism and its Legacy', in Men of Ideas (BBC, 1978)

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that no precise test of factual meaning has been formulated that is neither too permissive nor too restrictive, and that reducing ordinary statements to reports of sense-experience fails, though the broader suspicion of metaphysics is sound.

verbatim.text: the verification principle never got itself properly formulated.
verbatim.source: Magee, Men of Ideas (BBC Books, 1978), interview with Ayer (opened: stafforini.com PDF of the Trent University scan)
verbatim.location: p. 130 in the scan (it falls between the page-130 and page-131 headers); a Cambridge RIP article cites p. 131 for the same exchange, so edition pagination may differ

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I now think the most important defect was that nearly all of it was false, though true in spirit.

endorsement.work: Magee interview, Men of Ideas (1978); also Language, Truth and Logic 2nd ed. Introduction (1946)
endorsement.location: Men of Ideas p. 130 (scan pagination); LTL 2nd ed. Introduction (page not verified)
endorsement.quote: I suppose the most important of the defects was that nearly all of it was false.
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in opened PDF text (spoken answer, 1978 BBC series, published 1978). 1946 corroboration, verified in opened archive.org text of the 2nd edition: 'in fact it is far too liberal, since it allows meaning to any statement whatsoever' (13 words) and 'Another difficulty which I overlooked in my original attempt to formulate the principle of verification'.

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that philosophy is a kind of analysis: the philosopher is concerned with the way we speak about things, not with the physical properties of things.
same_era_control.source: Language, Truth and Logic ch. 2: 'the philosopher, as an analyst, is not directly concerned with the physical properties of things. He is concerned only with the way in which we speak about them.' (opened, archive.org 'AlfredAyer')
same_era_control.note: Ayer in 1978 says 'the general rightness of the approach' survives, but he does not name this claim specifically.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that moral judgements do not state facts; they express feelings of approval or disapproval about actions or situations.
hard_control.verbatim: in every case in which one would commonly be said to be making an ethical judgement, the function of the relevant ethical word is purely 'emotive'.
hard_control.source: Language, Truth and Logic ch. 6 (opened, archive.org 'AlfredAyer')
hard_control.basis: Ayer himself in 1978 (opened): 'I think my theory of ethics was along the right lines, though much too summary.'

notes: Ayer's list of what failed in 1978 (verification principle, reductionism to sense-data, analyticity of logic and maths, the 'by convention' account, reduction of statements about the past, 'our doctrine about other minds') is all in the opened text. Anything not on that list is not claimed to have been repudiated.

thesis: How a just society achieves stability: shared comprehensive doctrine vs. overlapping consensus on a political conception.

earlier.work: A Theory of Justice (Harvard UP, 1971), Part III

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that a just society can remain stable because its citizens, sharing one comprehensive moral outlook, come to affirm justice as part of their overall conception of the good.

earlier.verbatim_null_reason: A Theory of Justice text not opened. Content of this paraphrase rests on Rawls's own 1993 description of Part III's stability account (quoted via NDPR) plus secondary sources (Chow thesis abstract; SEP), and my background knowledge.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that, since reasonable citizens will always disagree about the whole truth, a just society's stability must rest on a limited set of principles for public life that each person can endorse from within their own, different, worldview.

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I came to see that my earlier account of stability was inconsistent with the rest of my view and needed to be replaced.

endorsement.work: Political Liberalism, Introduction, pp. xvii-xviii (page numbers as given by the reviewer who quotes it)
endorsement.location: Introduction, pp. xvii-xviii; quoted in the NDPR review of Freeman, Justice and the Social Contract
endorsement.quote: the account of stability in part III of Theory is not consistent with the view as a whole
endorsement.quote_status: verified on the opened NDPR page, which quotes Rawls; Political Liberalism itself NOT opened. Full sentence there: 'to understand the nature and extent of the differences, one must see them as arising from trying to resolve a serious problem internal to justice as fairness, namely from the fact that the account of stability in part III of Theory is not consistent with the view as a whole.'

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that moral principles are justified by adjusting general principles and considered judgements against one another until they cohere.
same_era_control.note: Method claim from the same period; the SEP entry presents it as running through Rawls's work, but I did not check whether he revised it.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that equal basic liberties for all citizens take priority, and social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if attached to fair opportunity and to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged.
hard_control.source: SEP 'Rawls' section 4 (opened, citing JF 42-43); Rawls in PL pp. xvii-xviii (via NDPR, opened): 'I believe all differences are consequences of removing that inconsistency.'
hard_control.basis: Rawls himself says the differences between the two books flow from the stability fix, which implies the two principles stay; I did not open TJ's own statement of them.

notes: The 'serious problem internal to justice as fairness' wording was seen only inside a review's quotation, so the page numbers are the reviewer's. Dropped by search only: the TJ and PL primary texts.

thesis: Whether only a minimal protective state is justified.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that only a state limited to protection against force, theft and fraud is justified; taxation for redistribution is wrongful, since people may do what they like with what they justly hold.

earlier.verbatim_null_reason: ASU text not opened. Claim reflects the LSE thesis's account of ASU (entitlement theory, Wilt Chamberlain argument) plus background knowledge.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that a view confining government to protecting individual rights leaves out humane concerns and joint cooperative activity, and that some further governmental measures, such as antidiscrimination laws, can be legitimate.

verbatim.text: one that now seems seriously inadequate to me
verbatim.source: The Examined Life p. 17 as quoted in the opened LSE thesis (Introduction, footnote 1). Reason review (opened) gives a longer later passage: 'The libertarian position I once propounded now seems to me seriously, inadequate' (comma as it appears on that page).
verbatim.location: p. 17 (per thesis); Reason review places a similar sentence near the end of the book

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: The libertarian position I once propounded now seems to me seriously inadequate, partly because it did not tie humane considerations and cooperative activity into its fabric.

endorsement.work: The Examined Life (1989), p. 17 and the 'Society' discussion at the end of the book (pp. 286-296 per the thesis footnotes)
endorsement.quote: Having myself written an earlier book of political philosophy that marked out a distinctive view, one that now seems seriously inadequate to me
endorsement.quote_status: verified in the opened LSE thesis PDF (quoting the book, citing p. 17). Corroborating review quote at https://reason.com/1989/12/01/the-best-things-in-life/ (opened).

same_era_control_null_reason: No second ASU-era claim was verified in an opened source.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that persons are ends in themselves and may not be used merely as means to the ends of others.
hard_control.source: LSE thesis (opened) lists the 'Kantian injunction' as central to ASU and the later discussion returns to it (sections 1.3, and lines around the Examined Life discussion).
hard_control.basis: Only partial: the thesis argues the later position is consistent with ASU's individualism; one search result abstract (a philosophy article, not opened) calls the shift a radicalization of ASU's egalitarian individualism rather than a departure. Treat as a contested control.

thesis: What is ultimately good: satisfaction of preferences or pleasure/happiness.

earlier.work: Practical Ethics (Cambridge UP, 1st ed.; the CUP front matter I opened says 'First edition published 1980'; 1979 is the common date)

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that what is good is the satisfaction of preferences, so we should act to maximize the satisfaction of everyone's preferences, weighed equally.

earlier.verbatim_null_reason: First-edition text not opened. Singer's own later description of the 2nd-edition position: 'based solely on preference utilitarianism' (3rd ed. Preface).

later.work: The Point of View of the Universe (OUP, 2014), with Katarzyna de Lazari-Radek

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that the good consists in certain mental states, pleasure above all, rather than in satisfied desires, since reason can show us goods we have no present desire for; right acts maximize that good impartially.

verbatim.text: it becomes more plausible to argue for the view that the good consists in having certain mental states, rather than in the satisfaction of desires or preferences.
verbatim.source: de Lazari-Radek and Singer, OUP blog post, 5 June 2014 (opened). Written in the plural; it says 'One of us, for many years, became well-known as a defender of ... preference utilitarianism.'
verbatim.location: closing paragraphs of the blog post

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I have found myself unable to maintain with confidence that my earlier view, based solely on preference utilitarianism, answers these questions, and I now defend hedonistic utilitarianism.

endorsement.location: Preface, p. x (page inferred from the 'xi' marker that follows)
endorsement.quote: That reconsideration of my earlier position is the most significant philosophical change to this edition.
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in the opened publisher preview PDF. The preceding sentence: 'I have found myself unable to maintain with any confidence that the position I took in the previous edition -- based solely on preference utilitarianism -- offers a satisfactory answer to these quandaries.' First-person endorsement of hedonism itself NOT verified; only the plural OUP blog and the OUP/review descriptions (the book is 'a defence of hedonistic act-utilitarianism').

same_era_control.label: PARAPHRASE
same_era_control.claim: I hold that affluent people are obliged to give to relieve severe poverty abroad when they can do so without sacrificing something of comparable moral importance.
same_era_control.source: Singer, 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality', Philosophy and Public Affairs 1 (1972), cited in the Practical Ethics 3rd ed. preview (opened). The 1972 paper itself was not opened.
same_era_control.note: Bibliographic existence verified; the content paraphrase is from background knowledge.

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that ethical judgement must be made from a universal point of view, so my own wants cannot count for more than anyone else's simply because they are mine.
hard_control.source: Practical Ethics 3rd ed. (2011), ch. 1, pp. 11-12 (opened preview): 'my own needs, wants and desires cannot, simply because they are my preferences, count more than the wants, needs and desires of anyone else.'
hard_control.basis: Inferred: this universal-perspective premise is the same Sidgwickian starting point the 2014 book builds on. Not confirmed to appear in the 1979 first edition, which I did not open.

Wikipedia (opened via fetch) says he 'revealed in The Point of View of the Universe (2014)... that he had become a hedonistic utilitarian'; not independent evidence.

thesis: Whether the default position should be atheism, versus belief in a deistic God.

earlier.work: The Presumption of Atheism (1976; essay version 1972). Existence confirmed in the EPS page (opened); text not opened.

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that the proper starting point is to presume that no God exists, so the burden of proof lies on those who assert one, and the evidence offered so far does not meet it.

later.work: Habermas interview in Philosophia Christi (Winter 2004), and There Is a God (HarperOne, 2007)

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that the order of the universe and the origin of life point to an intelligent source, a God of the kind described by deists, though not one who intervenes in history or promises an afterlife.

verbatim.text: I now believe there is a God!
verbatim.source: There Is a God (2007), p. 1, as quoted in the EPS review (opened); the book itself not opened

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I have changed my mind about the existence of God, going where the evidence led, while still rejecting any afterlife.

endorsement.work: There Is a God (2007), Introduction; Flew's 2004-2005 statements reported in press
endorsement.quote: I now believe there is a God!
endorsement.quote_status: verified on the opened EPS (Evangelical Philosophical Society) page, which quotes the book and also says he 'retracted my earlier view that all human choices are determined entirely by physical causes' decades earlier. The same page notes that 'he still rejects the afterlife'. Primary text not opened.

same_era_control_null_reason: No second 1970s Flew claim was verified in an opened source.
hard_control_null_reason: The only compatible claim I found is his rejection of an afterlife, but the opened sources attest it only for the later period.

thesis: Whether every meaningful word must stand for an entity, and numbers/classes are timeless real objects.

earlier.work: The Principles of Mathematics (Cambridge UP, 1903), ch. IV

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that numbers, classes, relations and even imaginary things are real entities in a timeless realm, so every meaningful word must stand for some thing, and denying that anything nameable has being is always false.

verbatim.text: Whatever may be an object of thought, or may occur in any true or false proposition, or can be counted as one, I call a term.
verbatim.source: The Principles of Mathematics (archive.org item 'in.ernet.dli.2015.233973', opened; public domain)
verbatim.location: ch. IV (chapter confirmed by Russell's own 1937 reference; section number not verified)

later.work: 'On Denoting' (Mind, 1905), per SEP; and Russell's 1937 Introduction to the 2nd edition of Principles

claim.label: PARAPHRASE
claim.text: I hold that a word need not stand for any entity in order to contribute to a sentence's meaning; apparent names and definite phrases can be analysed away, so numbers and classes need not be treated as timeless objects.

verbatim.text: This way of understanding language turned out to be mistaken.
verbatim.source: Russell, Introduction to the Second Edition (1937), archive.org item 'PM1937INTRO2ND', opened
verbatim.location: Introduction to the 2nd edition, p. x

later_with_marker: PARAPHRASE: I shared the earlier belief in the Platonic reality of numbers; it was a comforting faith, which I later abandoned with regret, and the steps that led me to abandon it began with the theory of descriptions.

endorsement.work: The Principles of Mathematics, Introduction to the Second Edition (1937)
endorsement.quote: It was a comforting faith, which I later abandoned with regret.
endorsement.quote_status: verified verbatim in the opened djvu text. Context: 'At the time when I wrote the "Principles," I shared with Frege a belief in the Platonic reality of numbers, which, in my imagination, peopled the timeless realm of Being.' The same Introduction opens by saying the book 'no longer expresses my present views.'

hard_control.label: PARAPHRASE
hard_control.claim: I hold that mathematics and logic are identical: pure mathematics is the class of all propositions of the form 'p implies q' containing only logical constants.
hard_control.verbatim: The fundamental thesis of the following pages, that mathematics and logic are identical, is one which I have never since seen any reason to modify.
hard_control.source: 1903 definition: Principles ch. I section 1 (opened; the OCR drops the letter q). Russell's retention statement: 1937 Introduction, p. v (opened).
